binders: Let V = {s : {0} → ℝ}, the one-dimensional real vector space represented by Fin 1 → Real, with coordinatewise operations and its finite product topology and norm.
Universally quantify q : ℝ → ℝ → V, with first argument spatial position and second argument time.
Universally quantify speed ∈ ℝ, a constant scalar defining F(s) = speed s.
Universally quantify qt, qx : ℝ → V, the supplied time-derivative and spatial-derivative fields at the selected time.
Universally quantify a,b,t ∈ ℝ and massRate ∈ V.
After all these data and hypotheses, existentially quantify one production function p : ℝ → V. This witness may depend on the preceding data, including t and the interval endpoints.
Inside each asserted local balance at x, existential derivative vectors u,v ∈ V may depend on x and the preceding data.
hypotheses: For every x ∈ ℝ, the function τ ↦ q(x,τ) has derivative qt(x) at τ = t.
For every x ∈ ℝ, the function ξ ↦ q(ξ,t) has derivative qx(x) at ξ = x.
qt is integrable with respect to μ on both (a,b] and (b,a], where μ = Real.measureSpace.volume.
qx is integrable with respect to μ on both (a,b] and (b,a].
The function M(τ) = ∫_a^b q(x,τ) dμ(x) has derivative massRate at τ = t.
The same function M has derivative ∫_a^b qt(x) dμ(x) at τ = t. In particular, uniqueness of derivatives identifies massRate with this integral.
massRate ≠ speed q(a,t) − speed q(b,t), as vectors in V.
conclusions: There exists a single p : ℝ → V satisfying all the following properties simultaneously.

For every x ∈ ℝ, there exist u,v ∈ V such that τ ↦ q(x,τ) has derivative u at t, ξ ↦ speed q(ξ,t) has derivative v at x, and u + v = p(x). Under the hypotheses, equivalently p(x) = qt(x) + speed qx(x) for every x.
p is integrable with respect to μ on both (a,b] and (b,a].
∫_a^b p(x) dμ(x) = massRate − (speed q(a,t) − speed q(b,t)).
p is not the identically zero function on ℝ: equivalently, there exists x ∈ ℝ with p(x)(0) ≠ 0.

It is false that for every x ∈ ℝ there exist u,v ∈ V such that τ ↦ q(x,τ) has derivative u at t, ξ ↦ speed q(ξ,t) has derivative v at x, and u + v = 0. Given the derivative hypotheses, this is equivalently the existence of a real x with qt(x) + speed qx(x) ≠ 0.
mathematical_definitions: For a vector-valued function f, ∫_a^b f dμ means ∫_(a,b] f dμ − ∫_(b,a] f dμ. This definition is oriented and does not require a ≤ b.
Interval integrability means integrability on both oriented half-open intervals, equivalently on (min(a,b),max(a,b)].

Every derivative is a classical derivative in one real variable at an unrestricted point. For a V-valued function f, derivative v at z means the difference quotient tends to v as a nonzero real increment tends to zero.

The spatial flux derivative differentiates the composite ξ ↦ F(q(ξ,t)); it is not a derivative of F alone. Because F(s) = speed s, the supplied spatial derivative gives this derivative as speed qx(x).
The two local predicates include derivative existence as well as the balance equation. Their derivative witnesses are not arbitrary values once the derivatives exist.
Vector equations and inequalities concern the single coordinate indexed by 0. No spatial coordinate is represented by Fin 1; spatial position is the separate real argument.
The displayed definition of Real.measureSpace selects an instance without exposing its measure. The notation μ retains that exact selected measure.
translation.proposition_plain_english: For every one-component real field q on real space and real time, every real constant speed, supplied derivative fields qt and qx, real endpoints a and b, selected time t, and one-component vector massRate, assume that q has time derivative qt(x) at t for every real x, that its time-t spatial slice has derivative qx(x) at every real x, and that qt and qx are interval integrable with respect to the selected real volume measure μ. Assume also that the oriented spatial integral M(τ) has both massRate and the oriented integral of qt as its derivative at t, and that massRate differs from speed q(a,t) minus speed q(b,t). Then there exists an interval-integrable spatial production function p such that, at every real x at time t, the time derivative of q plus the spatial derivative of its constant-speed flux exists and equals p(x). The oriented integral of p equals massRate minus the stated endpoint-flux difference. Moreover, p is not identically zero, and the corresponding equation with zero production does not hold at every real spatial point at time t.

restrictions_and_vacuity_risks: The target is restricted to a single state component. Although the local definitions permit more general finite state spaces, the theorem fixes Fin 1.
All spatial derivative hypotheses and local balance conclusions range over all of ℝ, not merely the interval between a and b.

The derivative and balance statements concern only the selected time t. There is no assertion of the equation over a time interval or of a single production function working simultaneously for all times.
speed is constant in space, time, and state. It is unrestricted in sign and may be zero; no nonlinear or variable-speed flux is quantified.

There is no assumption a < b or a ≤ b. Equal endpoints make M identically zero and the endpoint-flux difference zero, contradicting the mass derivative and defect hypotheses; the implication is therefore vacuous when a = b.
Interchange of time differentiation and spatial integration is explicitly assumed through a derivative statement, not derived from pointwise differentiability and integrability.

Spatial differentiability of q at time t implies continuity of that slice, but no joint space-time differentiability, continuity of qt or qx, or integrability of q at every nearby time is explicitly assumed.
The integral expression defining M is a total Lean expression. The statement does not separately assert ordinary integrability of every nearby-time spatial slice merely by writing that expression.

production ≠ 0 states nonidentity with the zero function, not positivity, nonvanishing everywhere, or a specified sign. The integral identity and defect additionally force its oriented integral to be nonzero.
The conclusion explicitly denies the zero-source equation globally in space. It does not explicitly name a failure point or restrict such a point to the integration interval.

The witness p is existentially introduced, not prescribed independently as physical data. Derivative uniqueness forces p(x) = qt(x) + speed qx(x), although uniqueness of p is not an explicit conclusion.
No nonnegativity of q, interpretation as physical mass density, boundary conditions, initial conditions, units, or separate constitutive law for production is encoded.
The local equations are classical pointwise equations. The proposition does not formulate a weak or distributional balance law.
